Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 108, verses 1–2:

﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar.﴾ ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.﴾

The opening of the speech with the emphatic particle (inna) serves to draw attention to the news and to indicate that it is something great, which in turn implies the exalting of the status of the Prophet (ﷺ), as was explained earlier in ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. The statement is framed as glad tidings and the initiation of a gift, not as a report of a gift already given.

The pronoun of majesty ("We") indicates a bestowal of a great favour.

Al-Kawthar: in the language it is a name for abundant good, formed on the pattern fawʿal. This pattern is, for the most part, found in non-derived nouns such as al-kawkab (the star), al-jawrab (the sock), al-hawshab and al-dawsar, and in non-derived nouns it does not indicate anything other than its named referent. Since the root letters ku-th-r (abundance) occur in it here, its form conveys the intensity of what it is derived from, on the basis that an increase in the form of a word indicates an increase in its meaning. For this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it as "excessive in abundance," and this is the best and most precise explanation given of it. A parallel is jawhar, meaning "brave," as if he confronts his enemy openly; and ṣawma'a (minaret/cell), derived from the description aṣma' (slender of limbs), since the ṣawma'a is slender, because its height exceeds its thickness.

A man who is the possessor of abundant good may be described as kawthar, by way of describing with a verbal noun, as in the verse of Labid in lamenting ʿAwf ibn al-Ahwas al-Asadi:

"And the possessor of Malhub: we were stricken by his loss, and at al-Ridaʿ there is another house, a kawthar."

(Malhub and al-Ridaʿ are both waters belonging to the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma.) He described the house as a kawthar. Al-Kumayt had this in mind in his praise of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

"You are abundant, O son of Marwan, and good; and your father, the son of the noble lineage, was a kawthar."

The river of Paradise was also named al-Kawthar, as in the hadith of Muslim from Anas ibn Malik mentioned earlier.

The early scholars (al-salaf) explained al-Kawthar in this verse with various interpretations, the most general of which is that it is abundant good. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: 'Some people say it is a river in Paradise.' He said: 'It is of abundant good.'" From ʿIkrima: al-Kawthar here is prophethood and the Book. From al-Hasan: it is the Qur'an. From al-Mughira: it is Islam. From Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash: it is the abundance of the Ummah. Al-Mawardi related: that it is elevation of remembrance, that it is the light of the heart, and that it is intercession. The statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) narrated in the hadith of Anas does not restrict the meanings of the word to what he mentioned.

What is intended by this report is the good tidings to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the removal of whatever may be in his mind from the saying of those who said of him: "He is abtar" (cut off). Thus the meaning of abtar was opposed by the meaning of kawthar, as a refutation of their saying.

His saying ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾ is a parenthetical clause, and the fa' (so) is for consequence following this good tidings: that he should thank his Lord for it, since prayer consists of actions and utterances that indicate the glorification of God and praise of Him, and that is thanks for His blessing.

It is fitting that the thanks be by increased devotion, in contrast to what the polytheists and others who uttered their ugly saying "he is abtar" had done to him as enmity. Prayer for God is thanks to Him and a vexation to those who forbid him from prayer, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 9], because they forbade him only from the prayer that is for the sake of God and not the worship of their idols. Likewise sacrifice is for God.

The shift from the pronoun to the apparent noun in ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, rather than "So pray to Us," is because of what the word "Lord" carries of an allusion to His deserving worship on account of His lordship, in addition to the abundance of His bounty.

The idafa of "Lord" (rabb) to the pronoun of the addressee is intended to honour and draw near the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it there is an indirect indication that He nurtures him and is kind to him.

It is evident that in the sequencing of the command to sacrifice together with the command to pray after His giving him al-Kawthar, there is a particularity that fits the purpose for which the surah was revealed. Do you not see that He did not mention the command to sacrifice together with prayer in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say, so glorify your Lord with praise and be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 97] in the surah of al-Hijr?

It appears that this is consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning the polytheists' prevention of him from the House at al-Hudaybiyya. God informed him that He had given him abundant good, that is, He had decreed it for him in the future, and He expressed it in the past tense to confirm its occurrence. So the meaning of the verse is like the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1], for it was revealed concerning the affair of al-Hudaybiyya. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to him: "Is this a victory?" He said: "Yes."

This returns to what al-Tabari narrated from the statement of Saʿid ibn Jubayr: that His saying ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾ is a command to pray, to sacrifice his offering, and to depart from al-Hudaybiyya.

The lam in "li-Rabbika" (to your Lord) indicates that he is to devote his prayer to God alone, so he does not pray to other than Him. In it there is an indirect allusion to the polytheists, that they pray to idols by prostrating to them and circumambulating around them.

The conjunction of "and sacrifice" (wa-nhar) with ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾ requires that its complement be assumed to be similar to the complement of ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, by virtue of what precedes it indicating it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hear them and see﴾ [Maryam: 38], meaning "and see by them." So the assumed meaning is: "and sacrifice for Him." This is an allusion to the nullification of the polytheists' sacrificing offerings to idols. If the surah is Meccan, then perhaps when the time of the Hajj drew near, and he used to perform Hajj every year before and after the mission, and he had hesitated about sacrificing his offerings in the Hajj after his mission, while he wished to feed the needy of Makkah and those who attend the season, and he was reluctant to share with the people of polytheism in their practices, God commanded him to sacrifice the offering for God and to feed it to the Muslims; that is, their sacrificing to idols should not prevent you from sacrificing while intending that what you sacrifice is for God.

If the surah is Madinan and its revelation was before the obligation of Hajj, then "sacrifice" is intended as the sacrifices on the Day of Sacrifice (ʿId al-Nahr). For this reason many jurists said that His saying ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾ means the ʿId prayer. This was narrated from Malik in explaining the verse, and he said: "Nothing has reached me about it."

From the command to sacrifice following the command to pray, they derived an indication that the sacrifice is after the prayer. On this basis, the command is to nahr rather than dhabh, although the sheep is preferable among sacrificial animals and it is not slaughtered by nahr, and although the Prophet (ﷺ) sacrificed only sheep. This is a preference for the word nahr, which is what is observed in naming the day of al-Adha "Yawm al-Nahr" (the Day of Sacrifice), and so as to include the sacrifices of the body and the offerings of the Hajj, or to include the offerings whose sending was halted on the day of al-Hudaybiyya, as you have learned above. The choice of nahr is further supported by observing the rhyme of the letter ra' in the surah. Early exegetes had other views on the explanation of (wanhar) that render it a rare word.

**[Page 576]**

This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*), which may be an independent new statement, or the clause may serve as a justification (*ta'lil*) for the particle *inna* (indeed), provided *inna* is not meant to refute a denial. Its use to express justification is common, as was mentioned earlier at the words of God Most High: ﴿They said: "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence contains a restrictive construction (*qasr*), a third-person pronoun, and the word *al-abtar* (the one cut off). This indicates that the intended purpose is to refute a statement issued by a specific person, and to quote the wording that is being refuted. Al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Al-'Ass ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi saw the Messenger of God ﷺ in the Sacred Mosque, near the gate of the Banu Sahm, and he spoke with him, while some of the chieftains of Quraysh were in the mosque. When al-'As came in to them, they said to him: 'Who was it you were speaking with?' He said: 'That one, the abtar.' The son of the Messenger of God ﷺ, 'Abd Allah, had died before that, after his son al-Qasim had died before 'Abd Allah. Thus, with the death of 'Abd Allah, the male line of his descendants ﷺ ended on that day. They used to describe anyone who had no son as abtar, so God revealed this surah." The restriction occurs in His words, ﴿Indeed, your enemy, he is the abtar﴾, because the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) restricts the attribute of being abtar to the one described, who is the enemy of the Prophet ﷺ. This is a restriction of the predicate to the subject (*qasr al-musnad 'ala al-musnad ilayhi*), and it is a restriction by reversal (*qasr qalb*), meaning: he is the abtar, not you.

*Al-abtar* (the one cut off): its literal meaning is the one part of which has been cut off, and it has become especially applied to an animal whose tail has been cut off. It is used figuratively for one who lacks what people consider good, by way of comparison to the animal whose tail is cut off, a comparison of an intellectual concept to a sensible one, as in the hadith: "Every matter of importance that does not begin with the name of God is *abtar*." It is said: *batara* (he cut) something, when he cut off part of it, and *batira* (with a kasra) like *fariha* (he was cut off), so he is *abtar*. It is also said of one who has no male descendants: he is *abtar*, by way of metaphor, an imagined comparison to a sensible thing. They likened him to the animal whose tail has been cut off, because his trace has been cut off in the imagination of the people of custom.

The meaning of *al-abtar* in the verse is: the one in whom there is no good. It is a rejection of the statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il, or of someone else, concerning the Prophet ﷺ. By this meaning, the description of al-'As or someone else as *abtar* is correct, rather than the meaning he himself intended, since he slandered the Prophet ﷺ by calling him *abtar*, that is, without descendants. This is because al-'As ibn Wa'il has descendants: his son 'Amr, the noble Companion, and the son of his son, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, the noble Companion, and 'Abd Allah has many descendants. Ibn Hazm said in *al-Jamharah*: "His descendants are in Mecca and in al-Rahat."

So God's words ﴿He is the abtar﴾: the form of restriction required the affirmation of the attribute of being abtar for the enemy of the Prophet ﷺ, and its negation from the Prophet ﷺ, and he is the abtar in the sense of the one in whom there is no good.

But since the description *abtar* in the verse was used in imitation of the statement of the speaker, "Muhammad is abtar," as a refutation of that statement, and since their custom in describing the *abtar* was that he is the one who has no male descendant, it is fixed that this refutation is a kind of the wise style (*al-uslub al-hakim*), which is addressing the listener with something other than what he expects, by directing his speech to a meaning other than what he intended, as an alert that what is more deserving is other than what he meant by his speech. Like the words of God Most High: ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: they are times for people and for the Pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189]. This is done by turning the speaker's intended meaning away from *abtar*, which is one without a male son, to what is more deserving of consideration, which is one lacking a share of good. That is: having no child does not diminish a person, because that does not return to a person as a deficiency in his qualities, character, or intellect. Suppose he was never given a child at all; people have only agreed to consider it a deficiency because of their desire for children, based on their social conditions at that time, which depended on physical effort. They seek male children hoping for help from them in old age, and this is something that may or may not happen. Or they seek the remembrance of a person after his death, and this is an imagined matter. The Prophet ﷺ, God had made him self-sufficient through contentment, and honored him with support. God gave him a tongue of truth which He did not give to anyone else of His creation. Thus it became clear that his essential perfection is what God knew in him, since He placed His message in him, and his accidental perfection is his Companions and his community, since God made him closer to the believers than their own selves.

In the verse there is a figurative beautifying device (*muhassin al-istikhdam al-taqdiri*), because the driving of the refutation by way of restriction, with the words ﴿He is the abtar﴾, is a negation of the attribute of *abtar* from the Prophet ﷺ, but in a meaning other than the one his enemy intended. This is *istikhdam* that arises from the form of restriction, based on the view that *istikhdam* is not confined to using a pronoun in a meaning other than that of its antecedent. Our teacher, the scholar Salim Abu Hajib, verified this and considered it an aspect of the conjunctive *waw* in the words of God Most High: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], because the conjunction is by way of repeating the governing element, so it is as if He said: "and the angels come," and this coming is different from the coming of God Most High. He said: "Al-Khafaji had preceded us to this, when he applied it to the exception particle in *Tiraz al-Majalis* in the verse of Muhammad al-Salihi, one of the poets of Syria:

*"The tale of my love is not abrogated (*manscukh*), except in the registers (*daftar*)."*

*Al-shani'* (the hater): the one who hates. It is an active participle from *al-shana'a*, which is hatred, and it is also said *al-shana'an*. It includes every hater of him among the people of disbelief. All of them are cut off from good as long as they harbor hatred for the Prophet ﷺ. As for those among them who became Muslims, some of them turned into love for him and pride in him.

**Surat al-Kafirun**

This surah is titled in the Qur'anic codices in our hands, old and new, and in most of the exegeses, *Surat al-Kafirun*, by adding *surah* to *al-kafirun*, with the nominative *waw* retained in *al-kafirun*, following the wording of the Qur'an that occurs at its beginning.

It occurs in *al-Kashshaf*, the commentary of Ibn 'Atiyyah, and *Hirz al-Amani* as *Surat al-Kafirin*, with the genitive *ya'* in *al-kafirin*, by adding *surah* to it, which means the surah of the mention of the disbelievers, or the address to the disbelievers. Al-Bukhari titled it in the Book of Exegesis of his *Sahih* as the surah of (﴿Say: "O disbelievers"﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1]).

In *al-Kashshaf* and *al-Itqan* it is said: This surah and the surah (﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]) are both called *al-Muqashqishatan*, because they cleanse from polytheism, that is, they clear one of it. It is said: *qashqasha* when he removed the illness.

It is also called the Surah of Sincerity (*al-Ikhlas*), so these two names are shared between it and the surah (﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]).

It is mentioned in Surat Bara'ah that the surah of Bara'ah is called *al-Muqashqishah* because it cleanses, that is, it clears one of hypocrisy. So this is shared among the three surahs, and it requires distinction.

Sa'd Allah, known as Sa'di, said, quoting Jamal al-Qurra': it is called the Surah of Worship. In *Basa'ir Dhawi al-Tamyiz* by al-Fayruzabadi, it is called the Surah of Religion.

It is Meccan by consensus according to the reports of Ibn 'Atiyyah and Ibn Kathir, though it is narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr that it is Medinan.

**[Page 580]**

It is counted as the eighteenth in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Ma'un and before Surat al-Fil.

The number of its verses is six.

**\* \* \***

As for the occasion of its revelation, as related by al-Wahidi in *Asbab al-Nuzul* and Ibn Ishaq in *al-Sirah*: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was circumambulating the Ka'bah, when al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn Wa'il confronted him. They were men of rank among their people, and they said: 'O Muhammad, come, let us worship what you worship for a year, and you worship what we worship for a year, and we will share the matter together. If what you worship is better than what we worship, we will have taken our share of it, and if what we worship is better than what you worship, you will have taken your share of it.' He said: 'I seek refuge in God from associating anything else with Him.' So God revealed concerning them ﴿Say: "O disbelievers"﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], the whole surah. The Messenger of God ﷺ went in the morning to the Sacred Mosque, where the chiefs of Quraysh were, and he recited it to them, and they despaired of him at that point." They proposed this to him only because they saw his eagerness that they should believe, so they hoped to make him slip into acknowledging the divinity of their idols.

Ibn 'Abbas related: "They despaired of him, and they harmed him and harmed his Companions."

By this the purpose of the surah is known, which is that it is the despair of the disbelievers from his agreeing with them in anything of their disbelief, by a decisive statement, firm in the present and the future, and that the religion of Islam does not mix with any part of the religion of polytheism.
